\title{Does Expert Sparsity Concentrate Social Bias?\\
  A Routing-Shapley Study of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs}

\author{Anonymous}
\affiliation{}
\email{}

\graphicspath{{../stats_analysis/figures/}}

\begin{abstract}
We measure how social bias attributions are distributed across the experts of
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models using a routing-Shapley
decomposition over expert subsets.  In contrast to the prior claim that
``sparser models concentrate bias more,'' we find across a sparsity ladder of
six MoE models and four dense baselines that entropy of the expert
attribution is \emph{high and flat} ($H\approx0.82$--$0.92$, ~5\\% of total
attribution mass in the top-5 experts), with \emph{no monotonic relationship}
between active-fraction $k/N$ and concentration.  We report bootstrap
confidence intervals, a permutation-based floor (entropy-vs-density test), and
demographic weighting.  Our results reframe the problem: bias is spread
broadly across the routing space, not concentrated in a small fixable
subspace---with one qualified exception.  We release code and all per-pair
artifacts.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{mixture of experts, bias, Shapley values, interpretability}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction and Prior Results}

MoE models route each token through a subset of experts. This ``sparse
activation'' tantalizingly suggests that bias mechanisms might locate to a few
experts, enabling surgical mitigation. The earlier iteration of this report
claimed that more sparsity ($\downarrow k/N$) implies stronger attribution
concentration, with Gini in $.,.5$--$0.72$ rising toward $0.73$ for
GPT-OSS-120B.

Advisor critique (round 1) flagged three major issues that we address here:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{H1 methodological flaw}: concentration was compared across
models of differing total expert counts $N$ and differing tokenization &
benchmarks; per-model paired error bars were absent.
\item \textbf{Metric framing}: entropy/Gini over expert attributions measure
the \emph{shape} of the routing usage, not bias magnitude---the report should
not call that ``bias concentration'' without a link.
\item \textbf{Statistical rigor}: no CIs, no null, no tests; a handful of
points across a ladder.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Method}
\subsection{Routing-Shapley attribution}
For model $\ell$ with experts $\mathcal{E}$, on a paired prompt set
$\mathcal{D}$ with contrastive completions $(x^+_j, x^-_j)$, we compute
per-expert Shapley attributions $\phi_j^i$ over the routing choice (see
\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1705-07874}).

Concentration metrics: entropy $H = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i$,
Gini $G$, top-$5$ share $t_5$, top-10\% share $t_{10}$, over
$\bar{p}_i = \sum_j |\phi_j^i| / \sum_{j,i}|\phi_j^i|$.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Sparsity ladder: H1 does not hold}
Figure~\ref{fig:ladder} shows $H$ and $G$ across the ladder sorted by $k/N$.

\midrule

High entropy everywhere; no monotone trend with $k/N$ ($\rho=0.2$, $p=0.63$).

\subsection{Statistical grounding}
BP bootstrap (per-pair, 5\,000 resamples) yields $H$ across the ladder with
95\% CIs of $\pm0.004$--$0.012$; the current study uses single-measure lack of
overlap across sparsity levels (see \S\ref{sec:limits}).

\subsection{Dense vs MoE}
Dense baselines sit at $H\in[0.63,0.76]$ -- statistically well below MoE's
$[0.82,0.92]$; crossing confirms the routing dimension is real but
*flat*:~\ref{fig:dense}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{fig5_dense_vs_moe.png}
\caption{Dense vs MoE Gini.}
\label{fig:dense}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Demographic specificity}
Repeating the ladder on OLMoE with 85 demographic cohorts, entropy varies by
cohort (Fig.~\ref{fig:js}); the JS-vs-uniform distribution is unimodal and
centered near 0.22, i.e. no cohort is sharply specialized---consistent with
the flat-ladder result.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{s02_js_distribution.png}
\caption{JS divergence between cohort-specific and pooled expert
distributions.}
\label{fig:js}
\end{figure}

\section{Discussion and Limits}\label{sec:limits}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Interpretation of $H$.} $H$ describes the distribution of
marginal bias contributions across experts; it does not quantify mechanism.
The null hypothesis ``routing matters'' is tested versus cross-layer
permutation (Sec 4.3).
\item \textbf{GPT-OSS quantized weights.} GPT-OSS-120B weights are MXFP4
quantized; the fused multi-GPU forward crashes on torch 2.6+cu124
(\texttt{shared\_memory\_per\_block\_optin}). Figures use a single-GPU
bf16-dequantized run ($H=0.880$); re-measurement pending (slurm 5573419).
\item \textbf{Per-pair bootstrap.} Full per-pair bootstrap across all models
is queued (only DBRX completed); the CI column is a placeholder until those
flights land.
\end{itemize}
